DOCUMENT:
S1: Architecture contains UI Component, Logic Component, Storage Component, Common Component, Test Driver Component, E2E Component, Client Component.
S2: TEAMMATES is a Web application that runs on Google App Engine (GAE).
S3: Given above is an overview of the main components.
S4: The UI Browser seen by users consists of Web pages containing HTML, CSS for styling and JavaScript for client-side interactions such as sorting, input validation, etc..
S5: This UI is a single HTML page generated by Angular framework.
S6: The initial page request is sent to the server over HTTP, and requests for data are sent asynchronously with AJAX.
S7: In the UI Server the entry point for the application back end logic is designed as a REST-ful controller.
S8: The main logic of the application is in POJOs (Plain Old Java Objects).
S9: The storage layer of the application uses the persistence framework provided by GAE Datastore, a NoSQL database.
S10: The following explains the use of the Test Driver.
S11: TEAMMATES makes heavy use of automated regression testing.
S12: Test data is transmitted using JSON format.
S13: TestNG is used for Java testing (all levels) and Jest for JavaScript unit-testing.
S14: HttpUnit is used to set up a simulated web server in servlet-level tests, where an actual web server is not required.
S15: The E2E end-to-end component is used to interact with the application as a whole with Web browsers.
S16: Its primary function is for E2E tests.
S17: Selenium Java is used to automate E2E testing with actual Web browsers.
S18: The Client component can connect to the back end directly without using a Web browser.
S19: It is used for administrative purposes, e.g. migrating data to a new schema.
S20: The Common component contains utility code (data transfer objects, helper classes, etc.) used across the application.
S21: The diagram below shows how the code in each component is organized into packages and the dependencies between them.
S22: logic, ui.website, ui.controller represent an application of Model-View-Controller pattern.
S23: ui.website is not a real package.
S24: It is a conceptual package representing the front-end of the application.
S25: The diagram below shows the object structure of the UI component.
S26: ui.website is not a Java package.
S27: It is written in Angular framework and consists of HTML, SCSS, and TypeScript files.
S28: The framework will build those files into HTML, CSS and JavaScript files ready to be used by standard Web browsers.
S29: The UI component is the first stop for 99% of all requests that are received by the application.
S30: Such a request will go through the following steps.
S31: First, request received by the GAE server.
S32: Second, custom filters are applied according to the order specified in web.xml, e.g. OriginCheckFilter.
S33: Third, request forwarded to a Servlet object as specified in web.xml for further processing, depending on the type of request.
S34: There are two general types of requests.
S35: The user-invoked requests and the automated (GAE server-invoked) requests, which are processed differently.
S36: User-invoked requests are all requests made by the users of the application, typically from the Web browser (i.e. by navigating to a particular URL of the application).
S37: The request will be processed as in the image.
S38: The initial request for the web page will be processed as follows.
S39: First, request forwarded to WebPageServlet.
S40: Second, WebPageServlet returns the built single web page (index.html).
S41: Third, the browser will render the page and execute the page scripts, most of the time requiring AJAX requests to the server.
S42: Subsequent AJAX requests sent to the server will be processed as follows.
S43: First, request forwarded to the WebApiServlet.
S44: Second, WebApiServlet uses the ActionFactory to generate the matching Action object, e.g. InstructorHomePageAction.
S45: Third, WebApiServlet executes the action.
S46: Fourth, the Action object checks the access rights of the user.
S47: If the action is allowed, it will be performed, interacting with the Logic component as necessary.
S48: Fifth, the Action packages and processes the result into an ActionResult object.
S49: The most common format is JsonResult (requests for obtaining data or processing existing data), and other formats are defined as necessary, e.g. FileDownloadResult (e.g. downloading feedback session report) and ImageResult (e.g. profile pictures).
S50: Sixth, WebApiServlet sends the result back to the browser which will then process it on the front-end.

DOCUMENT:
S51: Requests for static asset files (e.g. CSS, JS files, images) are served directly without going through web.xml configuration at all.
S52: The Web API is protected by two layers of access control check.
S53: These are origin check, authentication and authorization check.
S54: Origin check mitigates CSRF attack.
S55: Authentication and authorization check checks if the logged in user (or lack thereof) has sufficient privileges to trigger the API's actions.
S56: Special keys (csrf key and backdoor key) can be used to bypass each of the checks, typically for testing purpose.
S57: Those keys are strings known only to the person who deployed the application (typically, the administrator).
S58: Automated requests are all requests sent automatically by the GAE server during specific periods of time.
S59: This type of request will be processed as follows.
S60: First, the source of the request will be checked for administrator privilege.
S61: If this privilege is absent (e.g. non-administrator users trying to invoke the automated actions), the request will be dropped and a 403 Forbidden status will be returned.
S62: Second, requests generated by the GAE server are equipped with this privilege.
S63: Third, administrators can manually invoke these requests.
S64: This is particularly useful in testing the actions associated with those requests.
S65: Fourth, request forwarded to the AutomatedServlet.
S66: Fifth, automatedServlet uses the AutomatedActionFactory to generate the matching AutomatedAction object, e.g. CompileLogsAction.
S67: Sixth, automatedServlet executes the action.
S68: Seventh, the corresponding AutomatedAction will be performed, interacting with the Logic component as necessary.
S69: GAE server sends such automated requests through two different configurations.
S70: These configurations are cron jobs or task queue workers.
S71: Cron jobs are jobs that are automatically scheduled for a specified period of time, e.g. scheduling feedback session opening reminders.
S72: It is configured in cron.xml.
S73: Task queue workers are hybrids of user-invoked and GAE-invoked in that they are queued by users (i.e. users request for the tasks to be added to queue), but executed by GAE (i.e. GAE determines when and which tasks in the queue are executed at any point of time).
S74: This is typically used for tasks that may take a long time to finish and can exceed the 1 minute standard request processing limit imposed by GAE.
S75: It is configured in queue.xml as well as the TaskQueue nested class of the Const class.
S76: Since the high-level workflow of processing a request is same for any request (differing by the two request types only), we use the Template Method pattern to abstract the process flow into the Action and AutomatedAction classes.
S77: The Logic component handles the business logic of TEAMMATES.
S78: In particular, it is responsible for the following.
S79: Managing relationships between entities, e.g. cascade logic for create/update/delete.
S80: Managing transactions, e.g. ensuring atomicity of a transaction.
S81: Sanitizing input values received from the UI component.
S82: Providing a mechanism for checking access control rights.
S83: Connecting to GAE-provided or third-party APIs, e.g. for adding tasks to the task queue and for sending emails with third-party providers.
S84: Package overview contains logic.api, logic.core.
S85: logic.api provides the API of the component to be accessed by the UI.
S86: logic.core contains the core logic of the system.
S87: Logic API is represented by the classes Logic, GateKeeper, EmailGenerator, EmailSender, TaskQueuer.
S88: Logic is a Facade class which connects to the several Logic classes to handle the logic related to various types of data and to access data from the Storage component.
S89: GateKeeper checks access rights of a user for a given action.
S90: EmailGenerator generates emails to be sent.
S91: EmailSender sends email with the provider chosen based on the build configuration.
S92: It connects to the email provider by using the appropriate Service class.
S93: TaskQueuer adds tasks to the task queue.
S94: It connects to GAE's task queue API.
S95: To access control the following information are presented.
S96: Although this component provides methods to perform access control, the API itself is not access controlled.
S97: The UI is expected to check access control (using GateKeeper class) before calling a method in the Logic.
S98: To API for creating entities the following information are presented.
S99: Null parameters causes an assertion failure.
S100: Invalid parameters throws InvalidParametersException.

S114: This is because if it does not exist, it is as good as deleted.
S115: The following explains the Cascade policy.
S116: When a parent entity is deleted, entities that have referential integrity with the deleted entity should also be deleted.
S117: Refer to the API for the cascade logic.
S118: The Storage component performs CRUD (Create, Read, Update, Delete) operations on data entities individually.
S119: It contains minimal logic beyond what is directly relevant to CRUD operations.

S123: All GQL queries are to be contained inside the Storage component.

S134: Note that the navigability of the association links between entity objects appear to be in the reverse direction of what we see in a normal OOP design.
S135: This is because we want to keep the data schema flexible so that new entity types can be added later with minimal modifications to existing elements.
S136: Represented by the Db classes.
S137: These classes act as the bridge to the GAE Datastore.
S138: Add and Delete operations try to wait until data is persisted in the datastore before returning.
S139: This is not enough to compensate for eventual consistency involving multiple servers in the GAE production environment.
S140: However, it is expected to avoid test failures caused by eventual consistency in dev server and reduce such problems in the live server.
S141: Eventual consistency here means it takes some time for a database operation to propagate across all serves of the Google's distributed datastore.
S142: As a result, the data may be in an inconsistent states for short periods of time although things should become consistent eventually.
S143: For example, an object we deleted may appear to still exist for a short while.
S144: Implementation of Transaction Control has been minimized due to limitations of GAE environment and the nature of our data schema.
